sports.title: LeBron James Shrinks Scoring Role For 76ers Defense
sports.description: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images LeBron James is taking fewer shots than ever before in his long career, yet the Philadelphia 76ers are winning more games than any other team in the league. Through his first seven games, the four-time champion is averaging 15.7 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 7.4 assists. His field-goal attempts have dropped to just 13.1 per game, while his free-throw attempts sit at 4.4. These numbers mark the lowest pace for his scoring average and shot volume since he entered the NBA as a rookie. Instead of carrying the offense alone, James is now playing as a facilitator alongside a roster packed with elite scorers. On Wednesday night, Detroit Pistons fell 112-106 as the 76ers secured eight wins from their opening nine contests. This surprising drop in personal usage has allowed Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown to generate offense independently while James directs the flow. Defense Becomes the Team Identity While James cuts back on his scoring, the starting five has limited opponents’ scoring. The group has held teams to just 95.4 points per 100 possessions across their first five games together. For context, the league’s best defense before Thursday was allowing 103 points per 100 possessions. This gap shows how much the Sixers have improved on that end of the floor. James made the goal clear after the win over Detroit. After defeating the Pistons on Wednesday, “Our defense is going to be our identity,” James stated, according to NBC News . The starting lineup features James, Brown, Maxey, V.J. Edgecombe, and Joel Embiid, a group that combines for 36 All-Star selections. They have outscored opponents by 15 points in 77 minutes of play together. Cleveland Returns With a Different Star James faces his old team, the Cleveland Cavaliers, for the first time since choosing Philadelphia in free agency. During 11 Cleveland seasons, he guided the franchise to its initial 2016 NBA championship. The Cavaliers enter Friday with a 4-4 record after back-to-back losses to Oklahoma City. They also face injury concerns with key player Jarrett Allen listed as questionable for tonight’s game. Donovan Mitchell has averaged 22.5 points for Cleveland, but the team needs better collective production to beat Philadelphia. James Harden has struggled with his shooting efficiency. With the Eastern Conference’s top record, the 76ers have claimed five straight victories. James noted that his role has changed because he knows the team needs him to be ready for late-game situations. Patience Over Hype Despite the strong start, James warns against looking too far ahead at the end of the season. Regarding this talented group, certain fans propose an NBA Finals appearance is inevitable. sports.title: ‘Looks play a big part’: Former WNBA star explains why Sophie Cunningham is popular despite lackluster stats
sports.description: Aug 23, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham (8) reacts while warming up prior to a game against the Chicago Sky at Wintrust Arena. Mandatory Credit: Patrick Gorski-Imagn Images Caitlin Clark has become the face of the WNBA, and the Indiana Fever have become one of the league’s most popular teams because of her. But WNBA legend Angel McCoughtry thinks Clark’s teammate Kelsey Mitchell isn’t getting nearly enough credit. Appearing on the Get To The Point podcast with Terrell Owens and Chris Spencer, McCoughtry argued that looks play a bigger role in WNBA marketing than they do in other sports. She pointed to Mitchell as an example, saying that the Fever’s “best player” is barely recognized by fans. Mitchell’s Big Season Mitchell put together a terrific season for the Fever in 2026. She led the team in scoring, averaging 24.7 points per game, while Clark averaged 22.3 points per game. Mitchell has also been one of Indiana’s most consistent players in recent years, earning All-Star honors and serving as the Fever’s top scoring threat alongside Clark. Still, Clark is the one who draws the crowds and the endorsements. Her arrival turned the Fever into a national draw, and she has become one of the most marketable athletes in sports. ‘Looks play a big part’ McCoughtry, a five-time WNBA All-Star, said that she noticed the gap in attention firsthand. “In the NFL and NBA, if you’re good, you’re good. In the WNBA, if you look pretty… You might not be the best player…” McCoughtry said. “I went to a conference, and everybody loved Indiana. They love Caitlin Clark. I said, ‘How many of you know Kelsey Mitchell?’ None of them raised their hand. She’s the best player on the team,” McCoughtry said, on the podcast . “The leading scorer on that team. Only 100k. She don’t have a million followers.” Owens jumped in to ask if McCoughtry was suggesting that Clark is pretty. She declined to say that she was, but she then brought up Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, pointing out that she has an Adidas shoe deal despite averaging “nine points per game.” Cunningham actually averaged 7.9 points per game this season. McCoughtry said that there are other girls that are “balling” that don’t have similar deals. “Not the best player you’ve ever seen, but she’s getting the brand endorsements,” McCoughtry said. “In the woman’s game, is it really about how good you are or the visibility – how pretty you are?” “Yes, looks play a part. They play a big part,” McCoughtry said. Spencer went on to bring up other examples like Anna Kournikova and Michelle Wei, who weren’t the most successful in their sport but received brand sponsorships, potentially because of their looks. sports.title: Gateway Dirt Nationals Best Appearing Car Contest Returns In 2026 With Cash Prizes
sports.description: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The 2026 Gateway Dirt Nationals will give fans a direct say in which race cars look the best on the track. Organizers confirmed that the Best Appearing Car Contest returns this year for both the Super Late Model and Modified divisions. Two drivers will walk away with cash prizes, and the crowd gets to pick the winners. FloRacing and the event organizers plan to hand out $1,000 to the winner in each division. The money might seem small compared to the race purse, but the bragging rights are worth much more to the teams. Tyler Carpenter won the Super Late Model title in 2026, while Haleigh Gross took the award in the Modified class, according to FloRacing . Now the competition resets for a new year of paint jobs and creative designs. A Decade of Indoor Racing The race takes place inside The Dome at America’s Center, a venue that has hosted the event for ten years. This setting allows for unique paint schemes that might not survive on outdoor tracks. Drivers and teams arrive each December with eye-catching designs to grab the attention of the crowd. The contest celebrates this decade of racing indoors by rewarding the teams that put the most effort into their look. They will select 10 cars from each division to become finalists before the public votes. This step ensures that only the most impressive rides make it to the final round. Photo galleries featuring all 20 finalists will appear on FloRacing so fans can see the details up close. How the Voting Works Once the finalists are announced, the fans take control of the outcome. Supporters can visit FloRacing.com to cast their votes for their favorite cars. During the voting period, rules permit fans to cast up to four votes each day. This high volume of voting keeps the engagement high as the event gets closer. The specific dates for voting and other contest details will be released as the event approaches. FloRacing will broadcast all three nights of racing live for viewers who cannot travel to St. Louis. sports.title: NFL Rumors: Insider Sheds Light on Lamar Jackson’s Future with Baltimore Ravens
sports.description: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson suffered a severe thumb injury in Week 8 against the Buffalo Bills in his first game back after missing multiple weeks with an ankle sprain. While Baltimore just acquired Jacoby Brissett to fill the void at quarterback for the rest of 2026, questions remain about Jackson’s future with the franchise. Baltimore must figure out something with Jackson this offseason. The 2027 NFL salary cap is currently projected by OverTheCap.com to be $327 million. Jackson’s cap hit next season is too high for the franchise to justify, especially given the needs throughout its roster with aspirations to rebound as a playoff contender. Lamar Jackson contract ( Spotrac ): $84.34 million cap hit in 2027, $42.47 million dead cap in 2028 Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta’s options are further complicated by the contract extension he signed his MVP quarterback to in 2023. Jackson’s five-year deal included a no-trade clause, meaning that Baltimore needs his explicit approval to move him to another club. The franchise also can’t use the franchise tag on him in 2028 when he expires. That gives Jackson, who doesn’t have an official agent, complete leverage over the situation. Many in sports media and around the National Football League have speculated that the two-time NFL MVP and the storied franchise could potentially part ways after the 2026 season. However, that doesn’t seem to be the plan. Ahead of Baltimore’s Week 8 Thursday Night Football matchup against the Jacksonville Jaguars, NFL insider James Palmer reported on Amazon Prime Video that the Ravens are willing to make Jackson the highest-paid player in NFL history. When the Kansas City Chiefs reworked the Patrick Mahomes contract in June, the agreement added two years to his contract and made the average annual value a record-setting $64 million. Mahomes and Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott ($60 million AAV) are the only NFL players making $60-plus million per season. Ahead of his age-30 season, it stands to reason that Jackson would be looking for another five-year contract. Baltimore could tack four years onto his current deal, potentially at $65 million per season. It would make him the highest-paid player in NFL history, keep him under contract through his age-35 season and likely allow him to spend his entire career in a Ravens uniform. Silver Sluggers are not exactly the most precise way to define hitting excellence. That said, they still carry weight among the players themselves, however, as they are voted on among managers and coaches league-wide to determine which players were the ‘best’ hitters at their own positions during the most recent season. The Volunteers found a way to lose against South Carolina as the mistakes finally caught up with them late. The penalties have been a theme for Tennessee ever since Josh Heupel arrived in Knoxville. Heupel’s Tennessee teams have finished outside of the top 100 overall in penalties in four of his five seasons. 2026 has been no different. The Volunteers rank 100th in FBS with 61 penalties on the year. They’re 91st in penalty yards, checking in with 62.12 yards surrendered per game. Tennessee’s opponent this week, Kentucky, is 17th in the same statistic. That’s been a theme for Kentucky all season long — playing clean and taking advantage of opportunities. It’s something that quarterback Kenny Minchey can hang his hat on this year, throwing 14 touchdowns against just one interception. Kentucky has a turnover margin of +13 for the season. Tennessee is +3 in that category for the season. The Volunteers have turned the ball over 11 times on the season, with an opportunistic, aggressive defense propping up their overall margin. Kentucky has turned the ball over just five times all season. “Playing a really good football team that is playing extremely well together,” Josh Heupel said of Kentucky. “You look at their ability to win multiple ways, finish games. Turnover margin, they’ve been elite. One of the least-penalized teams in the league, playing really smart all three phases, so it’ll be a great test.” With an inexperienced quarterback making just his fourth start, keeping things on schedule is a must. The little things — the 3rd and 3 that turns into 3rd and 8 — those are the things that Tennessee really can’t afford down the homestretch, starting on Saturday night. The Volunteers are playing a defensive, ball-control brand this season, and that brand really needs clean football to be successful. We’ll see if Tennessee can clean things up against Kentucky on Saturday. Kickoff is set for 6:15 p.m. ET on ESPN.

technology.title: Mac lookalikes multiply as Linux raids Apple's wardrobe
technology.description: Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop. Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS , a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish , is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef . Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old. Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling , and Windows apps via Wine. This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux , a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition. What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience. Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urge among Linux users, and with legitimate reason. There's nothing wrong with Macs, even if you are mainly a FOSS user. Modern macOS, or OS X as it was called a decade ago, is a Unix underneath its shiny proprietary desktop, and many of the flagship Linux FOSS apps also have Mac versions, from Firefox and Thunderbird, via LibreOffice, to VirtualBox, plus less well-known but very handy apps such as Ferdium and Panwriter. We've written about the usefulness of FOSS apps on macOS before, including for reviving elderly Macs . Just a couple of months ago, we published a two-part guide on how to give Xfce a macOS-like layout and then how to tweak it so apps fit in better . We focused on the functionality, though, not the looks – we don't really care much for such things. If it does matter to you, though, you're not alone, and there are lots of themes and skins to make Xfce look prettier. Some of these are all-in-one packages that you can install on an existing distro to give it a new look. One recent example is Cupertino , developed with assistance from Claude. From a few years ago, there are Small Sur and Ventura-Xfce . From nine years ago, long pre-LLM, there is osXFCE . We can see the appeal. technology.title: Oak Ridge labs gets hybrid quantum-HPC system to test qubit error correction
technology.description: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) now boasts a system for research into quantum error correction, combining IBM quantum processors with a high-performance compute (HPC) system based on AMD silicon. The Quantum Science Center ( QSC ) at ORNL, funded by the US Department of Energy (DoE), unveiled what it calls a co-design platform for quantum error correction, marrying up quantum and HPC technology. While useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems always seem to be at least a decade away, there have been notable advances over the past several years in the field of quantum error correction, according to ORNL. These include early demonstrations of protecting quantum information from environmental noise, which can cause loss of the fragile quantum states needed for computations. "Solving the challenges of quantum error correction is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, which is a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory," said QSC director Travis Humble. IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta said that it was no longer a question of whether error correction works, but how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle challenging problems. "This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale," he stated. ORNL's new tool combines an IBM Quantum System Two, equipped with the latest 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 quantum processors , and Umbra, a classical HPC system powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators. According to AMD, the CPUs provide the orchestration and general-purpose performance needed to coordinate everything, while the GPUs accelerate simulation, optimization and the parallel scientific computations surrounding quantum workloads. Also part of the system are AMD Versal SoCs to provide the low-latency control, readout and decoding capabilities for the quantum circuitry. ORNL says that this brings together the computing infrastructure needed for quantum error correction in a single environment, and opens it up to more researchers than ever before. They will use it to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications in an environment built for quantum-centric supercomputing, an emerging paradigm where quantum processors (QPUs), CPUs, and GPUs work together as one system. IBM says that one promising approach the co-design platform cloud explore is hierarchical error correction. It describes this as using an inner code to protect qubits within a module, while an outer code wraps around the inner code’s logical qubits and adds a second layer of protection. This approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical error rate of one in a thousand, IBM research suggested. technology.title: RIP to the world’s ugliest car
technology.description: Elon Musk has hit the brakes on the Cybertruck, announcing on X that Tesla will wind down production at its Texas factory around mid-2027. Despite years of delays , the stainless-steel turd Musk claimed was a futuristic, apocalypse-proof tank straight out of Blade Runner is headed for a production wind-down after roughly four years, putting the Cybertruck alongside such automotive flops as the Edsel and the DeLorean. We can’t even put the Cybertruck on the same tier as the Ford Pinto, as that deathtrap was produced for a decade. The first Cybertruck lumbered off Tesla’s production line in mid-2023 before going on sale later that year , and it was practically right out of the gate that the problems began. Within months of the first deliveries, recall notices began piling up on the monstrosity. Trim pieces were flying off, internal components were failing, cameras were malfunctioning – all in all, the thing has faced 11 recalls since hitting the road in late 2023, most recently in April 2026, when a defect in brake rotors was found to potentially cause cracks that could allow wheel studs to separate from their hubs. Musk had pinned a lot of Tesla's hopes on the Cybertruck a few years ago, describing it during the company's Q3 2023 earnings call as "a great product" that would eventually generate "significant positive cash flow" for Tesla. Musk said on that same earnings call that Tesla intended to ramp Cybertruck production up to 250,000 vehicles per year by 2025 to meet the over one million Cybertruck reservations he claimed Tesla had taken. Some Musk fans may still be waiting for their Cybertrucks, while others may have canceled their reservations after reading early reviews or experiencing the reality of driving such an ugly vehicle associated with a right-wing provocateur. Tesla hasn't disclosed how many reservations were canceled or converted into sales. Even then, it was widely reported in recent years that unsold Cybertrucks were piling up around the US, with Tesla unable to move them even with repeated price reductions. Tesla has never shared Cybertruck sales numbers, but it’s estimated that only around 70,000 of the things have been sold in the past three years - not exactly a ringing endorsement of its marketability. So that’s that for the Cybertruck - it’s safe to say it’s been a total disaster for Musk and Tesla. It never sold well, never became a boat , and will likely never be remembered fondly. ®

science.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
science.description: null Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight. The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement . "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden." There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem. Telescopes their more stable digital twins The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors. This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image. To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani , and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets. science.title: Hera probe gets 1st good look at asteroid system clobbered by NASA's DART mission | Space photo of the day for Nov. 6, 2026
science.description: null The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system. "The first thing we said was, 'Wow,'" Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement about the image, which ESA released on Thursday (Nov. 5). "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world." What is it? The Didymos system consists of the eponymous 2,560-foot-wide (780 meters) space rock and its "moonlet" Dimorphos, which is about 530 feet (160 m) in diameter. The DART mission impacted Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, with the aim of causing a change in the orbital period of the moonlet. And it worked: Before the impact, Dimorphos completed one lap around Didymos in around 11 hours and 55 minutes. The DART collision reduced the length of this period by around 33 minutes. The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision. The newly released photo shows Didymos in detail. Just a sliver of Dimorphos is visible, below and slightly to the left of the main asteroid. Why is it incredible? The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach. Hera's observations should help reveal what other changes have occurred on and around Didymos. Scientists are already seeing that, while Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator as before the impact, many changes have occurred. This includes the creation of multiple boulders, craters, and patterns of grooves or ridges. "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 kilometer [0.62 miles] of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," said Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify." Stay tuned to Space.com for more Hera findings from Didymos.

science.description: null The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) . If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho. What is happening? The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun , a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings. And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way. The culprit is a large coronal hole in the sun, shaped a bit like a witch on a broom... (Image credit: NASA SDO) The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second. The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field , potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen. A predictive model from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center showing speedy solar wind (radial velocity image lower left) arriving at Earth (green dot) around Nov. 6 and persisting through Nov. 9. (Image credit: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center) Where will auroras be visible? Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat. But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field. science.title: 4-billion-year-old 'Rosetta Stone' found in Sahara Desert could unlock the secret history of water on Mars
science.description: null A rose-colored rock discovered in the Sahara Desert may hold some clues to Mars' ancient geological history. The meteorite , named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered in 2022, weighs roughly 1.8 pounds (800 grams) and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. Blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually landing on Earth, it is one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The extraordinary age and unusual mineral composition of Teghaza 001 offer a rare glimpse into the formation of Mars' early crust and how volcanic materials may have been altered by water, according to a statement from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” research leader Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California said in the statement. "One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars." A Rosetta Stone for Mars Unlike many Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 contains a distinctive combination of igneous minerals and textures that preserve evidence of its complex history. Its mineral composition resembles materials observed in Mars' southern highlands by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter . Although researchers can’t pinpoint exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, they have identified 13 potential locations on the planet where it may have formed. "This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before," team member Lee Saper, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, said. "It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." The meteorite was initially identified as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes. To determine its age, scientists then examined tiny zircon crystals embedded in the rock. Using a specialized rubidium-strontium dating technique, researchers analyzed individual mineral grains on its surface, preserving it for future analysis. 13 locations on Mars that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGS) The results revealed that Teghaza 001 was altered by water around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting the rock itself formed even earlier. The mineral and chemical evidence points to a dynamic water cycle on ancient Mars, when liquid water interacted with the planet's crust and potentially left traces of its atmosphere as it gradually lost water. Scientists believe further analysis of Teghaza 001 could reveal more about how water shaped the Martian surface and influenced the planet's evolution. The study also marks the first time researchers have used rubidium-strontium dating to analyze an ancient Martian meteorite , opening the door for the technique to be applied to other samples in the future. "We've only scratched the surface," Liu concluded.

science.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
science.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Taking a Gander at Utah’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 6, 2026 Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long, meandering path on its gradual journey downslope. But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. Some experts think that within the later stages of this “ still-enigmatic ” history, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the San Juan’s headwaters , which increased the river’s gradient and sped its flow. With that, the water’s erosive power intensified, and the river started carving its winding path deeper and deeper through 300-million-year-old rock. Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.” An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026. In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park , the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. In places, it nearly loops back on itself, making horseshoe-shaped bends. One section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies. Entrenched meanders in Utah’s Goosenecks State Park are bathed in golden light on August 8, 2016. Photo by Bob Wick (BLM) While the goosenecks are an unusual geologic wonder to behold by day, the area’s dark skies are a spectacle by night. Goosenecks State Park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. According to DarkSky International, features such as the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud in the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way are visible to the unaided eye from the park. In November 2026 , dark skies offer the chance to view several meteor showers, with the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids reaching their peaks throughout the month. science.title: 'We got it done!' Spacewalking astronauts finish installing next-gen ISS solar arrays
science.description: null Just as NASA is preparing to demonstrate " Max Power " on the ground, two astronauts on a spacewalk have provided the International Space Station (ISS) with the same. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency installed and deployed the eighth and final ISS Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) on Thursday (Nov. 5), augmenting the space station's legacy solar array wings to produce as much as 30% more electricity. "We got it done!" said Menon at the end of the 6-hour-and-59-minute spacewalk . The EVA (extravehicular activity) began at 8:36 a.m. EST and ended at 3:35 p.m. EST (1336 to 2035 GMT). NASA astronaut Anil Menon (at far right) is seen at the base of the newly-deployed eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) during a spacewalk on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Repeating many of the same tasks as they did on an Oct. 29 spacewalk that added the penultimate iROSA, Menon and Kutryk worked this time on the starboard side of the station's backbone truss on the 3B power channel. The two retrieved the 750-pound (340 kilograms) iROSA assembly from a temporary stowage platform, carried it to the worksite by way of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and mounted it to its previously assembled bracket kit. Menon then attached the cables to tie the iROSA into the station's systems but ran into a problem. "We are seeing half of the expected shunt current that we want," radioed Nichole Stilwell, a NASA astronaut serving as the spacewalk officer in Mission Control. "In this current config, we are not necessarily going to deploy." To address the issue, the connectors needed to be inspected. Out of safety concerns — given that the arrays generate electricity whenever lit by the sun — the astronauts needed to wait for the space station to enter the shadow of Earth to see what could be done. In the interim, they spent the time cleaning up their worksite and returning the Canadarm2 to its park site as they would have done after the deployment. Fortunately, they were able to clear the issue. "We are seeing good shunt currents on the ground, so we are go for deploy," said Stilwell. Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk (at center) works on mounting the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) during a spacewalk on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) After releasing two bolts, Kutryk and Menon watched as the array started to unfurl to its full 63-foot (19 meters) length. No motor was needed; the iROSA, as designed, used only the potential energy stored by its rolled-up carbon composite booms to extend itself. The entire process took about 10 minutes. "Today marks the completion of not just one solar array but, over 15 years after its development, eight arrays," said Menon at the close of the spacewalk. "These solar arrays are incredible. Half the size of the old ones and bringing 40% more power." NASA graphic showing the location and power channel

Jeff Bezos' company announced today (Nov. 5) that it has developed a third stage for its New Glenn rocket, which it says will make the powerful launcher more capable and flexible. science.title: The economic benefits of the covid vaccines may be double what we thought
science.description: The covid-19 vaccines were costly to produce, but paid for themselves many times over Paul Christian Gordon / Alamy The covid-19 vaccines may have provided health and economic benefits worth up to $64.3 trillion in the first year alone – almost double an earlier estimate. Previously, researchers calculated that the $79.4 billion invested in developing covid-19 vaccines saw a return of between $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion globally in the first 12 months after their rollout. But now, a reanalysis of the data suggests it is actually between $6.43 trillion and $64.3 trillion. This means that for every $1 spent on the vaccines’ development, between $59.70 and $809 was gained in that year. “It is great to finally see this research published to demonstrate the enormous health and financial benefits gained from covid-19 vaccines, in comparison to the costs that went into their development and delivery,” says Hallie Benjamin at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. Read more Does each new covid-19 variant pose a significant threat? The $6.43 trillion figure is based on a cost-effectiveness analysis that is generally used in the health sector and factors in quality of life, while the $64.3 trillion figure is based on a cost-benefit analysis used in the public sector. Advertisement Both include data from 173 countries on averted hospitalisations, productivity losses and lives saved. For instance, one of the estimates Benjamin and her colleagues used came from modelling that suggested the vaccines prevented 14 million to 20 million deaths in their first year. The initial $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion figures were released when the research was in a preprint stage, before it had been peer-reviewed. “We made many changes throughout the peer-review process that strengthened the quality of our findings,” says Benjamin. The researchers originally used the Value of Statistical Life Years, which considers how many years a person would be likely to live because of the vaccine, a figure that would be lower if someone was older. As part of the peer-review process, they were advised to use the Value of Statistical Life. Team member Mark Jit at New York University says this treats life spans more equally and is aligned with recommendations for valuing mortality-risk reductions. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The cost-benefit analysis figure also increased significantly due to a change from calculating the economic value of avoiding a death, says Jit. But the returns weren’t equally distributed. The researchers found that the vaccines had the highest returns in richer countries. This was probably because poorer countries accessed them later, so fewer lives were saved and fewer productivity and healthcare costs were averted, says Jit. The results are “a message about the need for being able to distribute the vaccines fairly to the people most in need around the world”, he says. Covid raises risk of heart issues in children

science.title: Tomb in Siberia reveals humans were using cannabis 2800 years ago
science.description: Researchers excavate a burial mound containing horse and human bones along with cannabis seeds Frozen Corpses Golden Treasures, T.Wallace & G. Casp A hair found in a 2800-year-old tomb in Siberia has yielded the earliest definitive evidence of cannabis being used as a psychoactive drug. But the history of such use is likely to go back much further. Genomic studies suggest that the domestication of cannabis plants ( Cannabis sativa ) was happening in China about 12,000 years ago , with people potentially exploiting it for oil and hemp fibre. Archaeological sites with artefacts made from hemp dating to 7500 years ago have been found in China and Japan . The earliest firm evidence of the plant’s use as a drug had been chemical traces on wooden braziers in China that implied humans were “smoking” cannabis 2500 years ago as part of funeral rites. Read more How a surge in ancient plagues 5000 years ago shaped humanity Now, Gino Caspari at the University of Bern in Switzerland and his colleagues have pushed the date back another 300 years with a find at the Tunnug 1 burial mound in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. Advertisement The royal burial mound dates to the time of the Scythians, nomads renowned for their military skills and horseback archery who spread across a huge swathe of Eurasia. In an excavation trench at the centre of the mound, Caspari and his colleagues recovered almost 1000 whole cannabis seeds. Radiocarbon dating indicated that they were deposited around the start of the 8th century BC, some 2800 years ago. He says we can’t say how the person consumed the drug – it might have been smoked or the seeds could have just been ingested. Given its presence in the burial mound, Caspari says the use of cannabis was probably related to a ritual funerary process. That could have been for a religious high, but he suggests there might have been a more sinister use. What were ancient humans thinking when they began to bury their dead? Claims that a small-brained hominin called Homo naledi buried its dead raise intriguing questions about ancient minds and why we engage in this peculiar practice The burial mound also contains the remains of dozens of sacrificed horses and some scattered human bones, which could be indications of human sacrifice. “If you’re trying to sacrifice a human, it might be easier if they’re not quite as resisting.
